name: Hydroxycitric acid (HCA)

lead: HCA is the main acid in the rind of the Garcinia cambogia fruit and is sold as a fat-loss supplement, often in fat-burner blends.
Trials are mixed: a 1998 JAMA trial found no advantage over placebo, and a 2011 meta-analysis found a small short-term difference of uncertain relevance.

paras: In the lab HCA inhibits ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme that supplies building blocks for fat synthesis. Whether this reduces body fat in people is what trials have tested.

A meta-analysis reported about twice the rate of gastrointestinal side effects. It is considered contraindicated in colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, and reviews of liver injury list Garcinia products.

lead: Hydroxycitric acid (HCA) is a derivative of citric acid found in the fruit rinds of tropical plants, most notably Garcinia cambogia (Malabar tamarind, also called G. gummi-gutta), and in roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa). [1][2][3] The (-)-isomer found in Garcinia is a competitive inhibitor of ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme that supplies acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis, which is the basis for its marketing as a fat-loss supplement. [2][4]

Human trials of Garcinia extract for weight loss have given mixed results. A 12-week randomised trial published in JAMA in 1998 reported no significant advantage over placebo, while a 2011 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials reported a small weight-loss difference of uncertain clinical relevance and more gastrointestinal adverse effects. [5][6][2] Reviews of liver injury cite Garcinia-containing products among implicated supplements, though HCA's specific role is unclear. [2]
infobox: Garcinia cambogia (G. gummi-gutta) fruit rind; roselle [2][3]
Competitive inhibitor of ATP citrate lyase (animal and lab work) [2][4]

paras: HCA exists as four isomers and in open and lactone forms. The (-)-isomer is the one found in Garcinia, where it is the principal acid of fruit rinds of G. cambogia, G. indica and G. atroviridis. [2][4] Garcinia rind is traditionally used as a sour flavouring in fish curries and in folk remedies for digestive complaints. [7]

Garcinia extract standardised for HCA is sold as a weight-management and fat-loss supplement, alone and in multi-ingredient products. [1][7] It has been researched in combination with niacin-bound chromium and Gymnema sylvestre. [8] Researchers have also studied the potassium salt of HCA in kidney stone chemistry. [9][10]

In the lab, (-)-HCA inhibits ATP citrate lyase, limiting acetyl-CoA availability for lipogenesis, and animal studies have reported effects on lipid metabolism. [4][2] Whether this translates to fat loss in people at supplement doses has been tested in the trials below.

The 1998 JAMA randomised trial in overweight adults tested Garcinia cambogia against placebo for 12 weeks and reported no significant difference in weight or fat mass loss. [5] A 2011 meta-analysis of randomised trials concluded that Garcinia extract produced greater short-term weight loss than placebo by a small margin, while noting that the clinical relevance was uncertain and that the trials were of mixed quality. [6] A review in American Family Physician in 2004 also covered HCA among common supplements. [11]
A 2015 overview of Garcinia cambogia in Fitoterapia summarised both the traditional uses and the weight-loss research. [7]

According to Wikipedia, a meta-analysis found gastrointestinal adverse effects roughly twice as likely among HCA users, and HCA is described as contraindicated in people with colitis or inflammatory bowel disease. [2] A 2024 review cited by Wikipedia states that Garcinia products may cause liver disease, though the scope of that review is wider than HCA alone. [2]
No forum threads were available for this entry. HCA is classed in the fat-loss category because of its use in fat-burner products.

Human studies include the 1998 JAMA randomised trial, a 2004 study of an HCA extract (HCA-SX) with and without niacin-bound chromium and Gymnema sylvestre, and a 2011 meta-analysis of randomised trials. [5][8][6] Registered trials have examined hydroxycitrate in kidney-stone urine chemistry, botanicals and satiety in obesity (terminated, 17 participants), Garcinia rind powder in prediabetic obese patients (90 participants) and supplements for insulin resistance (terminated, 8 participants). [9][10][12][13][14]
